title: How Vincent van Gogh’s Sister-in-Law Worked Tirelessly to Make Him Famous
description:
in Art, History |   	October 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

No artist, no mat­ter how soli­tary by nature, becomes a cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non
body:
in Art, History |   	October 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

No artist, no mat­ter how soli­tary by nature, becomes a cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non alone. That’s even true of such an iso­lat­ed fig­ure as Vin­cent van Gogh, whose death in obscu­ri­ty at the age of 37 left open the ques­tion of who, if any­one, would vouch­safe his paint­ings to pos­ter­i­ty. The sup­port of the artist’s younger broth­er Theo is often giv­en a good deal of cred­it for mak­ing his work pos­si­ble, and not with­out rea­son. What’s some­what less wide­ly known is that Theo, who’d long been in poor health, died less than a year after Vin­cen­t’s sui­cide. The work of ensur­ing the lat­ter’s lega­cy then fell to the for­mer’s wid­ow Johan­na Bonger — or per­haps she under­stood that if she did­n’t stew­ard it, nobody else would.
As Cindy Poh explains in the New­s­think video above, Bonger inher­it­ed a great many of van Gogh’s works and stored them away while devis­ing a plan to make them famous. Prac­ti­cal­ly going door-to-door — and some­times, it seems, lit­er­al­ly going door-to-door — she stayed engaged with the late Theo’s art-world con­tacts. She cut sweet­heart deals with muse­ums and even donat­ed art­works out­right, increas­ing their chance of pub­lic expo­sure. She orga­nized exhi­bi­tions every­where from Paris to Berlin to Lon­don to New York, the most piv­otal being one held at Ams­ter­dam’s Stedelijk Muse­um in 1905. The 484 works put on dis­play made it the largest van Gogh show in his­to­ry, a record it still holds today.


	

At that time, well before The Star­ry Night and Sun­flow­ers adorned cof­fee mugs in sub­ur­ban house­holds the world over, van Gogh’s art could still shock some crit­ics with its uncon­ven­tion­al­i­ty. Oth­ers, how­ev­er, showed signs of the enrap­ture­ment that Bonger must have sus­pect­ed would one day be pos­si­ble. Think­ing strate­gi­cal­ly, she pre­ferred to sell few­er pieces for high­er prices, pre­serv­ing the val­ue of his work and lim­it­ing its avail­abil­i­ty on the mar­ket. After her sec­ond hus­band’s death, she redou­bled her ded­i­ca­tion to the art that had become her life’s mis­sion, even trans­lat­ing and pub­lish­ing the hun­dreds of let­ters he’d left behind, most of which were sent to Theo. We’ve heard many artists described as mar­ried to their work, a cliché that applies well enough to Vin­cent van Gogh him­self. But to be mar­ried to one’s broth­er-in-law’s work is a rar­er thing indeed — and some­times a more impor­tant one.

title: Robin F. Williams Suspends the Allure and Horror of Technology in an Endless Loop
description: A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body. Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the
body:
A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body. Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the character grasps a navy phone and stares catatonically at the screen. A vibrant infinity symbol is superimposed on the scene, emerging as endless loops of energy and mesmerization from the device.
The all-too-relatable portrait is part of a suite of new works by Robin F. Williams capturing the omnipotent techno-dystopia we’re collectively barreling toward. Extrapolating on the ways humanity and machines merge, the Brooklyn-based artist presents a mystical vision of another world infused with pop culture and art history. 
“Merminator” (2026), oil on linen, 60 x 40 inches
“The Merminator,” for example, combines two characters of the ’80s—a cyborg assassin and a Disney princess—to form a metallic bot perched on a stone as it, like Ariel, peers toward a world it presumably longs to be part of and yet won’t be accepted in. 
There’s also “I Am Not a Robot,” a symmetric piece that takes cues in composition and color palette from the spiritualist abstractions of Hilma af Klint. The painting also draws from Boticelli’s “Madonna of the Pomegranate,” which presents the titular fruit as a visual metaphor for the human heart. In Williams’ iteration, though, the subject is the phone, radiating outward in place of the life-giving source.
Under the fitting title Act Natural, the body of work plunges into the uncanny without settling into the strange state of things. The too-sleek, frictionless world the artist portrays exudes the allure of technology alongside the immense horror it elicits.
P·P·O·W presents Act Natural as a pop-up at Frieze’s No. 9 Cork Street in London, where it’s on view through October 24. Explore more of Williams’ work on Instagram.

title: Massive King Ramses II Statues Unearthed in Egypt
description:
News
                The two sculptures were discovered after a citizen found a hieroglyph-etched stone on his property.
body:
News
                The two sculptures were discovered after a citizen found a hieroglyph-etched stone on his property.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            One of the two recovered stone-carved statues of King Ramses II, recently unearthed in the Nile Delta village and archaeological site of Behbeit Al-Hagar in Egypt (all photos by and courtesy the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities)
    
        
            The Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the discovery of the remains of two enormous statues depicting King Ramses II in the village of Behbeit Al-Hagar, a known archaeological site in the Nile Delta. The artifacts were uncovered after a citizen notified antiquities authorities about finding a stone with hieroglyphic inscriptions on his property.Behbeit Al-Hagar is best known for the ruins of the Iseion, an ancient Egyptian temple devoted to the goddess Isis.  Per the Ministry's press statement, the excavation yielded one carved stone head of Ramses II wearing the double crown that signified the pharaoh's unified rule over Upper and Lower Egypt. The head is around 5'3" (1.6m) tall, indicating that the height of the entire statue would likely have exceeded 27 feet (8.5m) — a scale connoting immense artistic significance. Remains of the upper portion of the statue's back pillar were also found nearby, bearing an inscription of the King's Horus name: “Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat.”One of two carved stone heads depicting King Ramses II of the New Kingdom

title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s Truth About America
description:
Art Review
                The beauty of the Native artist’s forms seduces, but the visual history of destruction is embedded in
body:
Art Review
                The beauty of the Native artist’s forms seduces, but the visual history of destruction is embedded into each element.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Cannupa Hanska Luger, “American Traditional” (2026) (all photos Hrag Vartanian/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Two years ago, I encountered the infamous 1892 image of two men with a hill of buffalo skulls at the Baltimore Museum of Art. It was covered by a small wall-mounted curtain designed by Yurok artist Stormi Turner, and it gave the image, still shocking after over a century of circulation, the depth of tragedy that it warranted. Part of the Preoccupied: Indigenizing the Museum exhibition, it was a way of acknowledging the care that such a crime demands, in the same way that human remains are shown in museums today, often with warnings, behind doors you must open, or under covers that you must actively remove to see. Turner’s intervention was a way to honor an animal that many Native American groups and communities lived in symbiotic relationship with for millennia. That image came back to me when I walked into Cannupa Hanska Luger’s newest exhibition, American Traditional, at Garth Greenan Gallery in Soho, where the artist sets aside the participatory, ceramics-heavy projects he’s best known for and arrives at something more declarative — a synthesis of wood, ink, and archive that is his strongest work yet.In Mari Sandoz’s The Buffalo Hunters: The Story of the Hide Men, first published in 1954, she explains that North American bison, also called buffalo, were far more numerous than humans on the continent and there was “apparently no disease on all the continent that threatened the buffalo in any number.” That charmed existence for the largest land animal on Turtle Island was interrupted by the eventual arrival of European settlers, who with their horses, guns, and railroads made their slaughter into an industrial-scale activity. Luger's “Requiem” (2026)Luger, who was born on the Standing Rock Reservation, places a black abstracted bison atop a blackened rendering of a 19th-century American wood dining table. An enrolled citizen of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation, he has deep roots on the Great Plains, and he knows the history of destruction that tore the bison from the tribes of the region that was, as Sandoz put it, “almost the sole subsistence of the Plains Indian — his shelter, clothing, food and fuel.” The Cree scholar Tasha Hubbard goes further than Sandoz was able to. For Plains nations the buffalo were kin, part of the First Peoples rather than a separate species, and the campaign against them was, in her account, a genocide carried out by proxy and a “second major wave of trauma for Plains Indigenous peoples,” after epidemic disease. The army said as much. Hubbard quotes Colonel Richard Irving Dodge’s advice to hunters — “every buffalo dead is an Indian gone” — and General Philip H. Sheridan understood it before the historians did. In 1875, when the Texas legislature proposed a bill to protect the bison, buffalo hunter John R. Cook recorded Sheridan’s objection: “These men [the buffalo hunters] have done more to settle the vexed Indian question than the entire regular army has done in the last thirty years … Send them powder and lead if you will, but for the sake of a lasting peace let them kill, skin and sell until the buffalo are exterminated.”Artist Cannupa Hanska Luger pointing at his work “Shoots Today, Kills Tomorrow” (2026)

title: Artavazd Pelechian’s Distant Connections
description:
Film Review
                Through his “distance montage” technique, the Armenian filmmaker’s masterpieces are built around imp
body:
Film Review
                Through his “distance montage” technique, the Armenian filmmaker’s masterpieces are built around impressions, not stories. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Still from We (1969), directed by Artavazd Pelechian, (all images courtesy New York Film Festival)
    
        
            Artavazd Pelechian said his piece, and his admirers have waited decades for the world to take notice. The Armenian filmmaker, active primarily during the Soviet era, has a concise oeuvre: 13 works, mostly shorts, with two features that barely crack an hour. Aside from 2019’s Nature, he has not released anything since 1994. International recognition came gradually, but it has grown enough that many of his films have received 4K restorations that premiered at different festivals over 2026. Recently, the Pelechian Project was showcased at the New York Film Festival (NYFF), with eight of the director’s restored works in the program.At the storied All-Union State Institute of Cinematography in Moscow in the 1960s, Pelechian and his peers studied the work of titanic Soviet directors like Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, and Dziga Vertov, who shaped cinematography and editing in cinema’s early days. Pelechian deviated from their example, developing an approach he described as “distance montage.” All his movies are montage-based, with intricate shot assemblages unified by distinct themes. Speaking with Scott MacDonald in the 1990s, Pelechian explained the distinction between distance montage and the familiar notion of a montage: In Eisenstein, every element means something. For me, the individual fragments don’t mean anything anymore. Only the whole film has the meaning. … Eisenstein saw editing as a means to get from here to there, [whereas] I see editing as a means for seeing where we are.Still from The Seasons (1975), directed by Artavazd Pelechian

title: The School of Art at the University of Arkansas Offers Tuition-Free Graduate Programs
description:
Announcement
                Applications are now open for the 2027–2028 academic year.
body:
Announcement
                Applications are now open for the 2027–2028 academic year.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            Graduate applications are now open at the School of Art at the University of Arkansas for the 2027-2028 academic year. Applications will be accepted through January 15, 2027. The School of Art, housed in the Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences, has four tuition-free graduate programs and offers graduate assistantships, stipends and scholarships, as well as access to funding for fellowships, research and travel grants and residencies. The school offers over $3.5 million in student support annually, which includes scholarships, conferences, research and travel funding.As the first graduate-level art education program offered in the state of Arkansas, the M.A. in Art Education is designed for students who are seeking to deepen their knowledge of theory and practice in art education. The program trains art educators to use interdisciplinary, collaborative teaching and research to benefit students across Arkansas and the world. Students will learn the practice of art education across a range of educational sites, such as schools, museums and communities.The M.A. in Art History, specializing in the study of the Arts of the Americas, boasts a unique formal partnership with Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art. Graduate students have access to internship opportunities, archives, and a network of curators from across the world. The program encourages emerging scholars to reimagine what art history can be through hands-on learning, theme-based curriculum and opportunities for travel where graduate students have previously assisted faculty at statewide symposia and in curatorial projects at the Venice Biennale.  Focusing on graphic and communication design, the Master of Design program prepares designers to build a better world through design and shapes students as designers by preparing them for emerging roles and educating them on designing with accountability. Graduate students have led professional development field trips for undergraduates to local design firms and have worked on design projects with local businesses like Houndstooth Clothing and the City of Fayetteville’s Arts & Culture Division. They have traveled for research projects, working with communities abroad in Bangladesh and Italy, among other countries.The M.F.A. in Studio Art is designed to give students the space to further hone their craft and to learn rigorous theoretical inquiry, social awareness and research. Studio Art students choose a concentration — ceramics, drawing, painting, photography, printmaking or sculpture + experimental media. Alumni have won prestigious awards such as the Guggenheim Fellowship and the National Council on Education for the Ceramic Arts Fellowship.In 2027, the School of Art will add a new facility, the Gallery + Foundations building, which will house new galleries where students can exhibit work, and house the student-run Sugar Gallery which allows for all graduate students to enhance both arts administrative and creative practices.Applications are open now until January 15, 2027. Visit art.uark.edu for more information or bring your questions to our School of Art Graduate Information Session at 5:30pm (Central Time) on October 28, 2026.

title: This Ron DeSantis Statue Can’t Take the Heat
description:
News
                The climate group 350 Action’s gallium statue began melting soon after being installed outdoors in Tallahas
body:
News
                The climate group 350 Action’s gallium statue began melting soon after being installed outdoors in Tallahassee on October 13.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            350 Action's "DENIAL" (2026) (photo courtesy 350 Action)
    
        
            A life-sized statue of Florida Governor Ron DeSantis began melting soon after the climate advocacy group 350 Action installed it in front of a crowd of DeSantis supporters in Tallahassee on Tuesday, October 13.The transformation of the gallium statue, aptly titled "DENIAL," into a skeletal base highlighted the elected official's longstanding rejection of climate change as Floridians prepare to vote for who will be DeSantis's successor on November 3. The statue's placard reads, "I am not a global warming person," quoting DeSantis's proclamation during his gubernatorial campaign in 2018, and includes a reference to his 2024 signing of House Bill 1645, an energy law that axed the phrase “climate change” from Florida statutes and ended requirements for state agencies to prioritize climate-friendly facilities, among other rollbacks. "Just as state legislation used bureaucratic language to erase 'climate change' from public law, we used civic branding to the public to witness climate reality firsthand," a 350 Action spokesperson and organizer told Hyperallergic. "The reaction speaks for itself: you can't deny the physical laws of nature, and you can't argue with the public record."
